turns.text: Great. Here's how the lesson works. You'll talk about your job and a recent project. I'll give you follow-up questions, and when you make a mistake I'll explain it and let you try again. Before we start, there's a short level check so I can adjust the lesson for you. Are you ready?

storedTranscript.text: Hello, James. I'm Ryota, and I'll be your English teacher today. We'll talk about your work and a recent project, practise the present perfect and the past simple, and finish with some optional pronunciation. Does that sound good? (いかがですか？)
Oh, uh, yes.

Great. Here's how the lesson works. You'll talk about your job and a recent project. We'll practise two grammar points: the present perfect, for experience that continues now, and the past simple, for finished events at a specific time. I'll give you follow-up questions, and when you make a mistake I'll explain it and let you try again. Before we start, there's a short level check so I can adjust the lesson for you. Are you ready?
Oh, yes.
Please answer in English, and don't worry about mistakes. I just want to see what you can already do, so the lesson fits you. First question: can you tell me a little about your job? What do you do?
I'm engineer.
Thanks, James. What kind of engineering do you do?
I make cars.
Nice, cars are a great field. What part of the car do you work on?
Uh, sorry.
No problem, James. Let me ask it more simply: which part of the car do you work on? For example, the engine, the body, or the electronics? (エンジン、ボディー、電子部品など、どの部分ですか？)
Uh, sorry, I don't understand.
Let me ask it more simply. Do you make the engine? Or do you make the body of the car? (エンジンを作っていますか？それとも、車のボディーですか？)
Uh, please repeat.
Of course. Which part of the car do you make: the engine or the body?
Uh, I
make car.

Thank you, James. So you make cars as an engineer. Today we'll use short, simple sentences about your job. (ここから仕事について話します。)

Now it's your turn. Can you say one sentence about your job, starting with "I work"?
I work here for 7 years.

Good, you told me how long you have worked here. Since you started in the past and still work here, we say "I have worked here for seven years." 「have worked」は、過去に始まって今も続いていることを表します。

Can you say that sentence once more?
I have worked here for 7 years.

Yes, that's right: "I have worked here for seven years." You started in the past and you still work here now.

Next is your job. Shall we go on, or do you have a question first?
Uh, yes.

Present perfect is next. Here is the form, and then I'll ask you a question.

Have you worked for your current company for a long time? Try starting with "I have worked…".
Uh, yes.
Good, so you have worked for your company for a long time. Please say it in a full sentence, starting with "I have worked…".
Uh, sorry. again?
Sure. Have you worked for your company for a long time? (会社でずっと働いていますか？) Start with "I have worked…".
Uh, yes. For 7 year.
Good, you've been with your company for seven years. Now say it as one full sentence with "have worked": "I have worked for my company for seven years."
Uh, time management.
Sorry, I didn't catch that. Please try the sentence again on your own, starting with "I have worked…". (もう一度、「I have worked…」で始めてみてください。)

Let me say it for you: "I have worked for my company for seven years." Listen to how "have worked" connects to the time from the past until now.



That's the present perfect for now. Next is the past simple, for things that finished at a specific time.




Did you attend any business events or exhibitions last year? Just say "yes" or "no" for now.
Uh, helps me build more cars.
That's a good reason to study English, James. Now, please say your sentence again on your own: "I have worked for my company for seven years." (もう一度、自分で言ってみてください。)
It has helped me build more cars.

Yes, "It has helped me build more cars." is correct. You used has with a past participle for something that continues now. 「has + 過去分詞」で、今も続いている経験を表せています。

Now the past simple, for things that finished at a specific time. Please answer this question: did you attend any business events or exhibitions last year?
Yeah, quite a few actually attended, maybe about six exhibitions throughout the year.

Your sentence is correct: "attended" is the past simple, and "last year" tells us the events are finished. (「attended」は過去形で、「last year」は終わった時間を表します。)

Which exhibition was the most useful for your work? Try starting with "I attended…".
Yes, I attended about six exhibitions last year.

Yes, "I attended about six exhibitions last year." That's exactly right, and it's a finished time in the past. 「last year」は終わった時間なので、past simple を使います。

Now one more with "have worked", on your own. How many years have you worked as an engineer? Start with "I have worked…".
Uh, next.
Right, let's move on. For the open conversation, tell me about a project you're proud of, using the past simple.
I worked on a project with a new car that can actually fly.

Wow, a car that can fly! Your sentence is correct: "I worked on a project" is past simple, because the project is finished. (「worked」は過去形で、プロジェクトは終わっていますね。)

What was your job on that project? Try starting with "I was…".
Uh, yes, I did. There was about uh, 10 other engineers involved in the project.

Good, you worked with about ten other engineers. One small thing: with plural engineers, we say "were": "There were about ten other engineers." (エンジニアは複数なので、was ではなく were です。)

What was your own job on the project?
Uh, Comdex in Los in Las Vegas was great because it was very informative and very modern.

Comdex in Las Vegas sounds very interesting, James. "It was great" is correct, because "was" is the past of "is" and the event is finished. (「was」は過去形です。)

When did you go to Comdex? Try starting with "I went to Comdex in…".
The largest or the biggest challenge was finding the technology allowing the car to lift off the ground.

That's a clear answer, James. "Was finding the technology" is correct, and it shows the challenge was in the past. One small thing: we say either "the biggest challenge" or "the largest challenge", not both. (「biggest」か「largest」のどちらか一つで十分です。)

How did you solve that problem? Try starting with "We…".
The future of technology and AI.
Did you mean the future of technology and AI? Is that part of your project? (プロジェクトのことですか？)
The speed of change.
Thanks, James. Was the speed of change another challenge in your project? (プロジェクトで、変化のスピードも大変だったのですか？)
It definitely has. Um, I think less.

Yes, I understand. The speed of change was less of a challenge than the technology. Because the project is finished, we say "It was a challenge," not "It has been." (プロジェクトは終わっているので「was」を使います。)

How did your team handle the speed of change? Try starting with "We…".
It's helped me be more efficient with my time.

That's correct, James: "It has helped me be more efficient with my time." You used "has helped" for an effect that continues now. (「has helped」は今も続いている効果を表します。)

Now a short question: which part of your work is more efficient now? Try starting with "I am more efficient at…".
Uh, move on.
Okay, let's move on. Would you like to practise your pronunciation? (発音の練習をしますか？) You can choose single words, a whole sentence, or skip it.
Please move on to pronunciation practice.
Let's do it. Would you like to practise single words, or a whole sentence? (単語か、一文か、どちらがいいですか？)
Uh, just a little bit of individual words.
Let's start with one word. Listen, then repeat after me: responsibilities.
I said individual words.

Understood, James. I can't check the sound of your voice today, so I'll move on to the summary.

Shall we go on, or do you have a question first?
How much longer is this is this lesson?
We have about seven minutes left, so there's time to keep going. Let's go back to your project. How did your team handle the speed of change? Try starting with "We…".
Sorry, I have to finish now.

Understood, James. Today you practised "I have worked for seven years" and "I attended about six exhibitions last year," and you described your engineering project well. Keep using "have worked" for things that continue now, and "attended" for finished events. Thank you, and goodbye!
